# Chevy Malibu 2009 Won't Start: Diagnosing a Smoke-Filled Starter Scenario

Your 2009 Malibu isn't just refusing to start; it is exhibiting classic signs of an electrical cascade failure triggered by a primary component shorting out. The sequence you describedâa whining noise followed immediately by engine stoppage and a burning smellâis the mechanical equivalent of a server crash dumping core memory before the logs can even flush to disk. You correctly identified that jumping the battery yields no response other than a starter solenoid click, which isolates the issue to the high-current draw circuit rather than simple state-of-charge depletion.

The "whining" sound you heard likely wasn't the alternator bearing itself failing initially, but rather the alternator attempting to drive a seized internal rotor or a shorted diode pack that instantly overloaded the system. When an alternator develops a short in its stator windings or the diodes fail, it can draw hundreds of amps from the battery. In your specific case, this surge likely caused the engine control module (ECM) to cut fuel injection to protect itself, creating the "engine stop" event while the starter solenoid still had enough residual charge to click but not enough torque to crank the motor.

The burning smell under the hood is a critical diagnostic vector. While you suspect the alternator, you must also rule out the serpentine belt shearing off due to that sudden thermal spike or an overheated power steering pump bearing grinding against the pulley. If the belt snapped, it would explain why the water pump stopped circulating coolant (leading to overheating smells) and why the alternator is no longer charging, but it wouldn't necessarily prevent the starter from turning unless the accessory load caused a voltage sag that confused the ECU's start logic.

Before condemning the alternator based on symptoms alone, you need to verify the voltage drop across the starter solenoid while someone attempts to crank the engine with good jumper cables connected directly to the battery terminals. If the battery is healthy (12.6V at rest) and the starter solenoid clicks but the motor doesn't spin, measure the voltage at the starter's small terminal (S terminal). If this reads near 0V while cranking, your ignition switch or the neutral safety switch has failed to complete the ground circuit. If it reads 12V+ with no crank, the starter motor itself has seized internally, likely due to heat damage from the initial alternator failure.

To confirm the alternator is the root cause versus a secondary effect, disconnect the negative battery terminal and try to spin the alternator pulley by hand. It should rotate freely without grinding noises or excessive resistance. If it feels gritty or binds, the bearings are shot. Furthermore, check for smoke or melted plastic on the rear of the alternator housing where the field wire connects; this indicates an internal short that drew excessive current, causing the insulation to melt and the smell you detected.

Replacing the alternator is the logical first step, but be prepared that if the belt was under extreme heat when it snapped, the tensioner may also be compromised. Many 2009 Malibus use a hydraulic or spring-loaded tensioner; inspect the arm for cracks or signs of leaking fluid. If you replace the alternator and the whining returns immediately, the issue has migrated to the water pump or another accessory driven by the same belt.

Finally, ensure your starter solenoid is not sticking. The "click" indicates the coil is energizing, but if the plunger isn't fully engaging the main power contacts, you get a spark without rotation. Tap the starter body gently while someone tries to crank it; if it suddenly engages, the internal armature is worn and needs replacement. Don't ignore the burning smell, as that suggests active arcing or melting insulation that could lead to a fire if left unaddressed.
